title: Medusa
description: A poem from The World's Wife (1999) in which Medusa speaks in the first person about the jealousy that turned her hair to snakes and her eyes to stone, and about the love that keeps her dangerous.
plot_or_argument: Medusa begins with the origin of her condition: 'A suspicion, a doubt, a jealousy / grew in my mind, / which turned the hairs on my head / to filthy snakes / as though my thoughts / hissed and spat on my scalp.' The poem follows the transformation through her body - her breath souring, her lungs 'grey bags', her mouth foul, her teeth yellow fangs, 'bullet tears' in her eyes - and then turns to the man she loves: 'Be terrified. / It's you I love, / perfect man, Greek God, my own; / but I know you'll go, betray me, stray / from home.' She imagines the women he will look at, and what will become of them; she tells him that she is not the monster he thinks, that the stone is the hardening of a love that has been hurt. The poem's final movement is a warning and a confession: the gaze that petrifies is the gaze of someone who has been betrayed and will not be looked at again, and the poem's bitterness is directed as much at the woman's own jealousy as at the man.
narrative_structure: Seven stanzas of free verse, the first of five lines and the rest of six, without a regular rhyme scheme but with strong internal rhyme, assonance and consonance; the poem moves from diagnosis to transformation to address to warning, and ends on an image rather than a statement.
meter_and_prosody: Blunt, monosyllabic, deliberately ugly diction in the transformation stanzas ('foul mouthed', 'yellow fanged') set against the plain tenderness of 'It's you I love'; heavy alliteration and sibilance; short lines and hard enjambments; the tone is jeering, wounded and seductive at once.
historical_context: The World's Wife (Picador, 1999) is Duffy's best-selling collection, a series of dramatic monologues in which the wives and women of myth, history and literature answer back; 'Medusa' belongs to its sequence of classical and biblical retellings, and the collection was written in the years before Duffy became Poet Laureate in 2009.
literary_significance: One of the most widely taught poems of The World's Wife and a standard example of the feminist revisionary myth poem; it is one of Duffy's four selections in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The World's Wife (London: Picador, 1999). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning at page 1160.
thematic_analysis: Duffy rewrites the Medusa myth as the story of a woman destroyed by jealousy rather than by a curse: the snakes are her thoughts, and the petrifying gaze is the hardening of love into suspicion. The poem belongs to The World's Wife's project of giving the women of myth and history their own voices, and it makes a feminist argument about the way women are turned into monsters by the fear of betrayal, while refusing to excuse the violence that Medusa's own suspicion produces. The direct address to the lover makes the poem a love poem as well as a curse, and the imagery of the body - breath, lungs, eyes, teeth - keeps the myth physical.
summary: A dramatic monologue in seven stanzas of free verse, in which Medusa describes her transformation, addresses the man she loves, and warns him - and the reader - not to look at her.
research_notes: The poem's opening and several lines were read through the annotation page cited, which prints the text and describes the seven-stanza structure; it was not read complete from the printed collection.

title: Mrs Lazarus
description: A poem from The World's Wife (1999) in which the wife of Lazarus describes her grief, her slow recovery and remarriage, and the ruin brought back when her husband is raised from the dead.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins in the extremity of grief: Mrs Lazarus shrieks, tears her hair, lies on the grave, and performs the mourning that is expected of her, 'howling' and 'shrieking' until she has no voice left. Then the poem's time begins to move: she takes off her black, goes back to work, learns to sleep alone, and eventually meets another man and marries him. Duffy compresses the years - 'I would have to ask / how long' - and shows the recovery as unspectacular and physical: the body's habits changing, the house rearranged. The last two stanzas bring the miracle: Lazarus returns, and his wife, who has grieved him properly and buried him and made a life, is left with a husband she no longer knows and a new husband she cannot keep. The poem's final image is of the two men and the woman between them, and of 'the hours I had' - the life she had built - being taken back.
narrative_structure: Eight five-line stanzas of free verse, with no rhyme scheme; the poem is chronological, moving from the death to the mourning to the remarriage to the return, and its stanzas shorten and quicken as the miracle approaches.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, first-person, colloquial free verse with a strong physical vocabulary (shrieking, howling, the taste of ash, the smell of the grave); short sentences and abrupt line breaks; a tone that moves from raw grief to domestic calm to a final, quiet horror.
historical_context: The World's Wife (Picador, 1999) reworks the stories of women attached to famous men, from Mrs Midas to Mrs Darwin and Queen Herod; 'Mrs Lazarus' takes the raising of Lazarus in the Gospel of John (11:1-44) as its source and extends the four days of the biblical narrative into years, so that the wife's remarriage becomes credible.
literary_significance: One of the most frequently taught poems of The World's Wife and a set text in British schools; it is one of Duffy's four selections in the Norton Anthology and the collection's clearest example of its method of giving the untold woman's side of a familiar story.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The World's Wife (London: Picador, 1999). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning at page 1161.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the work of mourning and the way a miracle can be a catastrophe: Lazarus's resurrection, which the Gospel treats as a sign of divine power, is experienced by his wife as the destruction of the life she has slowly rebuilt. Duffy gives the woman the time the biblical narrative does not - the years of widowhood, the second marriage - and makes her grief a process with stages rather than a tableau. The poem is also about the social performance of mourning: the shrieking and hair-tearing that begin it are what is expected, and the poem's interest is in what comes after the performance ends.
summary: A dramatic monologue in eight five-line stanzas of free verse, in which Mrs Lazarus moves from frenzied mourning through the routines of widowhood to a new life, and then confronts the returned Lazarus.
research_notes: The account follows the annotation page cited, which prints the poem's opening stanzas and describes its eight-stanza structure and its departure from the Gospel narrative; the poem was not read complete from the printed collection.

title: Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard
description: An extract from Kiran Desai's first novel, Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard (1998), in which Sampath Chawla, a clerk who has climbed a guava tree in a Shahkot orchard, is discovered there and turned by his family and the town into a holy man.
plot_or_argument: Sampath Chawla, the son of Mr and Mrs Chawla of Shahkot, has failed at school, at his job in the post office and at the marriage his parents arranged for him, and has run away to live in a guava tree in a ruined orchard on the edge of town. The family finds him there: 'Searching for Sampath, the family clacked about the trees and shouted up into the leaves, the three women uttering his name with mournful wails, Mr Chawla shouting like an Army major.' A doctor is consulted and a debate follows over whether Sampath is mad - 'Is he biting his neighbors? Biting himself? Is he sleepwalking? Does he stick out his tongue and roll his eyes? Is he rude to strangers?' - and the answer, that he eats and sleeps and is polite, settles that he is not. The orchard, however, has other visitors: the townspeople, hearing of the man in the tree, begin to bring offerings; and the extract follows the first pilgrims, the gifts of food and money, the raising of a cot and an umbrella into the branches, and the transformation of a failed clerk into a guru whose answers - nonsense delivered with the authority of revelation - become 'the sermon in the guava tree'. The extract ends with Sampath installed in comfort, and with the town's credulity and his family's enterprise in full flood.
narrative_structure: A novel in thirty-odd short chapters, comic and episodic, with a large cast and a narrator who moves between the family's perspective and the town's; the Norton extract is a continuous sequence from the middle of the novel, covering the search, the diagnosis and the first devotees.
meter_and_prosody: Exuberant, comic, over-heated prose with long lists, exclamations and sudden lyric passages; a strong sense of place (the orchard, the town, the railway) and a taste for the absurd; dialogue in an Indian English with a vivid demotic energy, and a narrator who shares the characters' excitability.
historical_context: Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard was published by Faber and Faber in 1998 and won the Betty Trask Award; it was begun while Desai was studying creative writing in the United States, and it draws on her childhood in India and on the tradition of Indian comic fiction. 'The Sermon in the Guava Tree' was printed in The New Yorker in June 1997 as an extract from the then forthcoming novel, and the Norton Anthology reprints a passage of the same material.
literary_significance: Desai's first novel and the book that made her name before The Inheritance of Loss won the Booker Prize in 2006; the guava-tree episode is the novel's central comic idea, and the extract is her selection in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Faber and Faber (London) in 1998. Norton prints an extract under the title 'The Sermon in the Guava Tree', beginning at page 1200; a version of the same material appeared under that title in The New Yorker, 23 June 1997. This record covers the whole novel.
thematic_analysis: Desai's comedy is about the manufacture of sanctity: Sampath is a holy man because he is sitting in a tree and because a town needs a holy man, and the novel's satire is directed at the commercial and religious appetite that produces him. The orchard is also an ecological subject - a remnant of greenery that the town's traffic, rubbish and advertisements gradually overrun - and Sampath's retreat into it is a retreat from the noise of post-independence India into a silence he cannot keep. The family's eagerness to profit from his new status, and the bureaucracy's attempt to manage it, make the novel a study of how private eccentricity is converted into public property.
summary: A comic sequence from the novel: the Chawla family's search for Sampath, the discovery of him in the tree, the debate over whether he is mad, the arrival of the first devotees, and the beginnings of the 'sermon in the guava tree' that makes him a celebrity.
research_notes: The plot of the extract follows the New Yorker text (its opening and the quoted exchanges) and the summaries of the novel in the scholarly and reference sources cited; Desai's own date of first publication for the novel (1998) and the extract's New Yorker appearance (June 1997) are taken from those pages. The novel was not read complete.

title: Signs and Symbols
description: A short story first published in The New Yorker on 15 May 1948, under the title 'Symbols and Signs', and collected in Nabokov's Dozen (1958): an elderly émigré couple travel to a sanatorium to visit their mentally ill son on his birthday, are turned away after he has tried to kill himself, and return home to a telephone that will not stop ringing.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with the couple on a suburban train on a Saturday in April, carrying a small jar of beach-plum jelly as a birthday present for their son, who has been in a sanatorium for three years. The mother has brought a photograph, a pair of slippers and a comb as well, and worries about the weather and about what the doctor will say. At the sanatorium a nurse tells them that the boy has again attempted suicide - he has tried to throw himself out of a window - and that they cannot see him that day. On the train home the father, who is ill and short of breath, says that they must take him out of the place; the mother, who knows the boy's fear of strangers and of unfamiliar rooms, says nothing. At their apartment they eat a poor supper and the father dozes. The telephone rings: a girl's voice asks for 'Charlie', and the mother explains that it is a wrong number. It rings again, the same girl, the same mistake. Then, in the story's last line, it rings a third time and the mother, unable to bear it, tells her husband not to answer it. Between these events the narrator gives the boy's case history: his 'referential mania', in which 'the patient imagines that everything happening around him is a veiled reference to his personality and existence', and in which 'everything is a cipher and of everything he is the theme'; his terror of being watched by things rather than people; his drawing, his reading and the way he checks the water in the glass beside his bed. The parents' history is given in the same flat, exact detail: the flight from Russia after the revolution, the German maid in Berlin, the relatives murdered in the Holocaust, the rich brother Isaac who pays for the sanatorium, the nephew who is a famous chess player. The story ends with the third ring, and nothing is explained.
narrative_structure: Three numbered sections, each a single continuous movement: the journey out and the failed visit, the journey home and the evening, and the three telephone calls; the narration is third-person and external, moving without comment between the parents' errands and the case history of the son, so that the reader is given no more than the characters can see and no less than the story's pattern requires.
meter_and_prosody: Nabokov's English prose at its most exact and least ornamental: short declarative sentences, precise physical detail (the 'little jar' of jelly, the wet lilac, the 'dead leaves' of the suburban platform), dialogue reported without gloss, and a flat tone that refuses both sentiment and explanation; the story's horror is produced by the accumulation of ordinary detail, and its final sentence ('a third time, and she said: Don't answer it') is left to do the work of the ending.
historical_context: Written in English in 1948, the year Nabokov began teaching at Cornell, and published in The New Yorker on 15 May 1948 under the title the magazine's editor Katharine White preferred, 'Symbols and Signs'; Nabokov restored his own title and the numbered sections when he collected the story in Nabokov's Dozen (Doubleday, 1958). Its émigré couple belong to the world of Nabokov's Berlin and Paris stories, and its account of the Holocaust's reach into an ordinary family belongs to the first postwar decade of American fiction.
literary_significance: One of Nabokov's most anthologised short stories and the one most often used to introduce his fiction to students, since it displays in miniature his method of the 'second story behind the story', his interest in pattern and interpretation and his unsentimental tenderness; it is his selection in the Norton Anthology, where it opens the American volume's postwar section.
bibliographical_notes: First published as 'Symbols and Signs' in The New Yorker, 15 May 1948; collected as 'Signs and Symbols' in Nabokov's Dozen (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1958). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is a study in interpretation: the son's disease is the reader's own condition, since the story is made of details that seem to ask to be decoded - the jelly, the photograph, the girl asking for Charlie, the numbers of the sections - and Nabokov said that a 'second (main) story' was woven behind the 'semitransparent' one without saying what it was. The predominant reading is that the story traps us into the very over-reading it describes, so that the reader's hunt for a message is a milder form of the boy's referential mania. Behind that formal joke lies a real subject: the grief of exile, the Holocaust that has taken the family's other relatives, the poverty of the émigrés and the helpless love of parents who cannot reach a child who cannot bear to be looked at.
summary: Three numbered sections, running to some four thousand words, in which the third anniversary of the son's confinement, a failed visit, a birthday present, a train journey back to the city and three telephone calls at the end of the evening carry almost the whole of the story; its subject is the couple's poverty, their exile and their son's 'referential mania', a delusion that everything in the world is a coded message about him.
critical_context: Criticism has divided between readings that try to decode the story - arguing that the son has died, or that the third call is from him, or that the details hide a Holocaust allegory - and readings, now predominant, that see the story as a trap for exactly that kind of decoding: Alexander Dolinin and Brian Boyd have written on its many-layered structure, and the essay by Alexander Drescher on the 'beech plum' and the number of paragraphs is the best-known attempt to show that Nabokov did plant a code. Nabokov's own letter to Katharine White, describing 'a second (main) story ... placed behind the superficial semitransparent one', is the starting point of almost all of this criticism.
research_notes: The plot is summarised from the published story as described in the sources consulted and from the story's critical literature; the story itself was not read complete, and the quotations are those reproduced in the Wikipedia article on the story and in the criticism cited.

title: Cuttings
description: A nine-line poem from The Lost Son and Other Poems (1948), the first of the greenhouse poems, in which a tray of plant cuttings pushing out roots and a single pale shoot is watched with the attention of a naturalist and the awe of a mystic.
plot_or_argument: 'Sticks-in-a-drowse droop over sugary loam, / Their intricate stem-fur dries; / But still the delicate slips keep coaxing up water; / The small cells bulge.' The poem begins in exhaustion and dryness - the cuttings are sticks, half asleep, their fine hair dried out - and then, in the second sentence, something continues: the slips 'keep coaxing up water', the cells 'bulge', and a 'nub of growth / Nudges a sand-crumb loose, / Pokes through a musty sheath / Its pale tendrilous horn.' The whole poem is nine lines long, with no rhyme and no regular metre, and its movement is from the passive to the active, from the sticks lying on the surface to the single shoot breaking out of the soil; the verbs do the work - 'coaxing', 'nudges', 'pokes' - and they are all verbs of a gentle, persistent pressure rather than of force. Nothing in the poem is explicitly human, and nothing is explicitly symbolic: the shoot is described as an animal horn and as a 'nub', and the reader is left to feel the analogy with any beginning that has to push through something dry.
narrative_structure: A single sentence of four short lines followed by a second of five, unrhymed and unmetred; the line breaks isolate the verbs and the nouns of growth, so that 'One nub of growth' stands alone as a stanza of its own and the last three lines slow into the single image of the horn.
meter_and_prosody: Extremely compressed free verse, with heavy stresses and consonantal crowding ('Sticks-in-a-drowse', 'stem-fur', 'musty sheath', 'tendrilous horn'); the diction mixes botanical exactness with invented compounds and a faintly archaic formality; there is no simile and no moral, only the observation and the rhythm.
historical_context: The Lost Son and Other Poems (1948) gathered the greenhouse poems Roethke had been writing since the early 1940s about his father's and uncle's florist business in Saginaw, Michigan, and it made his reputation; the sequence's short 'Cuttings' poems stand at its head, and its longer title poem follows the same material into a child's night-time journey.
literary_significance: One of the best-known short poems in twentieth-century American poetry and the standard introduction to Roethke's greenhouse sequence; it is paired in the Norton Anthology with 'Cuttings (later)', and the two poems are the usual demonstration of how his close observation turns into myth.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Lost Son and Other Poems (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1948). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The greenhouse poems take the smallest possible subject - a cutting, a root, a weed - and treat it as a whole world, and 'Cuttings' establishes the method: exact notation of the physical, and then a leap, by image alone, into the human. The poem's interest is in the persistence of life in cut material, which is to say in growth that has been separated from its source and must make a new one, and in the way the poem's own attention ('coaxing', 'nudges') models the patience it describes.
summary: Two unrhymed sentences of observation: the cut stems droop over the loam and their 'stem-fur' dries, yet the slips keep drawing water and their cells swell, until one 'nub of growth' nudges a crumb of sand aside and pokes its pale horn through the soil.
critical_context: Readings of the greenhouse poems emphasise Roethke's combination of botanical precision with a psychological and religious charge: the plants are both plants and figures for the poet's own buried life, and the sequence has been discussed in relation to his biography (the father's greenhouses, the deaths of 1923) and to his reading of Jung and of the mystics. 'Cuttings' is usually treated as the purest example of the sequence's method, since it offers no explicit interpretation at all.

title: Cuttings (later)
description: The companion poem to 'Cuttings' in The Lost Son and Other Poems, in which the rooting of the same cut stems becomes a 'resurrection' that the poet feels in his own veins and that drives him back to 'beginnings'.
plot_or_argument: 'This urge, wrestle, resurrection of dry sticks, / Cut stems struggling to put down feet, / What saint strained so much, / Rose on such lopped limbs to a new life?' The first sentence turns the botany into hagiography: the cuttings are martyrs, their roots are 'feet', and the question is what saint ever rose on 'such lopped limbs'. The second sentence moves from observation to identification: 'I can hear, underground, that sucking and sobbing, / In my veins, in my bones I feel it, - / The small waters seeping upward, / The tight grains parting at last.' The poem ends with the shoot breaking the surface: 'When sprouts break out, / Slippery as fish, / I quail, lean to beginnings, sheath-wet.' The word 'quail' is both the bird and the flinch, and 'sheath-wet' carries the botanical sheath, the animal afterbirth and the poet's own body into a single adjective; the poet is not the observer of the growth but is implicated in it, and the poem's last gesture is a leaning backwards, towards what is beginning rather than what has grown.
narrative_structure: Eleven lines in two sentences, broken into a question of four lines, an account of five, and a final three-line movement; the line breaks fall on the verbs of growth and the last line is left short and exposed, so that the poem ends at the moment of breaking out.
meter_and_prosody: Heavier and more incantatory than 'Cuttings': the opening line crowds three abstract nouns and a noun phrase ('urge, wrestle, resurrection of dry sticks') into one breath, alliteration and assonance bind the lines ('sucking and sobbing', 'seeping upward'), and the diction runs from the colloquial to the liturgical ('What saint strained so much').
historical_context: Published beside 'Cuttings' in The Lost Son (1948), the poem belongs to the greenhouse sequence that established Roethke's reputation and to the postwar American poetry of the family and the unconscious; its language of resurrection and of 'beginnings' anticipates the long 'lost son' poems that follow it in the same volume.
literary_significance: The second of Roethke's paired 'Cuttings' poems and the one usually taken to show the mystical and autobiographical turn of the greenhouse sequence; the two poems together are the standard anthology selection from The Lost Son.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Lost Son and Other Poems (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1948). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: Where 'Cuttings' watches, this poem enters: the resurrection of the sticks is felt 'in my veins, in my bones', and the language of rooting becomes the language of birth and of resurrection, so that the poem's subject is the continuity between the vegetable and the human body. The word 'resurrection' also brings the poem's religious ambition into the open: the greenhouse is a place where the dead are made to live again, and the poet's response - 'I quail' - is a mixture of awe, fear and desire to be returned to the beginning, which is the emotional core of the whole greenhouse sequence.
summary: Eleven lines in two sentences: the 'urge, wrestle, resurrection of dry sticks' is compared to the straining of a saint, and the poet, hearing the 'sucking and sobbing' underground, feels the small waters seeping upward in his own bones and is left 'sheath-wet', leaning to beginnings.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as the point where the greenhouse poems become explicitly about the poet: the 'saint' and the 'resurrection' have been related to Roethke's reading of the mystics and to the death of his father, and the final 'lean to beginnings, sheath-wet' is often quoted as the sequence's statement of its own backward-looking method.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in the anthologies and study sources consulted; unlike 'Cuttings' this poem is less often reproduced complete, and the quotations were checked across two transcriptions.

title: The Waking
description: The title poem of The Waking (1953), which won the Pulitzer Prize in 1954: a villanelle in which the poet accepts that he wakes and sleeps 'by God's grace' and learns 'by going where I have to go', using the repetitions of the form as the vehicle of a mystical submission.
plot_or_argument: 'I wake to sleep, and take my waking slow. / I feel my fate in what I cannot fear. / I learn by going where I have to go.' The poem's opening sentence sets out its paradox: waking is a kind of sleep, and the way to learn is to go where one is compelled to go, without knowing where that is. The second stanza takes the same three propositions a step further - 'We think by feeling. What is there to know? / I hear my being dance from ear to ear' - and adds the strange, joyful image of the body's being dancing between the ears. The third stanza invokes God and asks for the grace of 'the deep' and of 'the clear', and the fourth and fifth return to the themes of darkness, light and the humility of not knowing: 'Of those so close beside me, which are you? / God bless the Ground! I shall walk softly there, / And learn by going where I have to go.' The final stanza gathers the refrains: 'Great Nature has another thing to do / To you and me; so take the lively air, / And, lovely, learn by going where to go. // This shaking keeps me steady. I should know. / What falls away is always. And is near. / I wake to sleep, and take my waking slow. / I learn by going where I have to go.' The last line of the poem, the refrain released from the tercet and left standing alone, is the poem's whole argument: knowledge is not acquired by understanding but by consenting to the way one is already going.
narrative_structure: A villanelle of six tercets in which line one and line three of the first stanza become the alternating refrains, and a final quatrain repeats both; the refrains are varied slightly - 'where I have to go' becomes 'where to go' - and the rhymes are carried by assonance and half-rhyme (slow/go/know, fear/ear/clear/near, air/there) rather than by exact rhyme.
meter_and_prosody: A spoken, almost conversational iambic pentameter with heavy monosyllables ('This shaking keeps me steady. I should know.'), colloquial contractions and exclamations set against a liturgical refrain; the diction is plain and the syntax short, so that the poem's profundity comes from repetition and from the pressure of the form rather than from ornament.
historical_context: The Waking: Poems 1933-1953 (1953) collected the three earlier books with new poems and won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1954; the title poem, written in the early 1950s, belongs to the period of Roethke's most concentrated religious poetry and to the American postwar vogue for the villanelle, which he helped to revive in English.
literary_significance: Roethke's best-known poem after 'My Papa's Waltz' and the one for which he won the Pulitzer Prize; it is a standard anthology piece and the demonstration text for the modern American villanelle, and its refrain 'I learn by going where I have to go' is among the most quoted lines in twentieth-century American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Waking: Poems 1933-1953 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1953). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: 'The Waking' is a religious poem that refuses doctrine: its God is invoked in the third stanza only to be left unnamed, and its 'Great Nature' does the work that providence does in a metaphysical poet. What the poem asks for is a way of living without certainty - 'We think by feeling. What is there to know?' - and its answer, repeated five times in the refrains, is that one learns by going. The villanelle's obsessive return of the same two lines is the poem's meaning as well as its form: a mind that cannot get past its own propositions and finds in the repetition not monotony but steadiness, and the paradox 'This shaking keeps me steady' names the comfort the form gives.
summary: Six three-line stanzas with the two refrains of the villanelle, in which the poet says that he wakes slowly and fears to wake, that he hears his fate in what he cannot see, that 'we think by feeling', that God's grace keeps him waking and sleeping, and that 'This shaking keeps me steady. I should know.'
critical_context: The poem has been read as a mystical text - Roethke's interest in Meister Eckhart, Jakob Böhme and the via negativa is well documented - and as a formal triumph in which the villanelle's repetitions enact the submission the poem describes. Critics have also written about its relation to Roethke's manic depression, reading 'This shaking keeps me steady' as a statement about the illness as well as about the verse, and the line has become a touchstone in discussions of the poet's late style.
research_notes: The poem was read through the text reproduced in the anthologies and study sources consulted, and the quotations were checked against more than one transcription; the critical material is paraphrased from general accounts and was not read in the specialist literature.

title: Elegy for Jane
description: An elegy from The Waking (1953), subtitled 'My Student, Thrown by a Horse', in which a teacher mourns a girl he loved 'in the way a father loves a daughter' and asks the natural world to remember her.
plot_or_argument: 'I remember the neckcurls, limp and damp as tendrils; / And her quick look, a sidelong pickerel smile; / And how, once started, she would never finish / Such waltzing ways.' The poem opens with the physical memory of the girl in the classroom: the damp hair, the fish-like sidelong smile, the restless movement. The second quatrain places her among the other students - 'She was not sparrow, starling, wren, or lark' - and the third gives her the poem's benediction: 'For nothing can assuage my grief / That such a one should be / Thrown by a horse.' The middle stanzas call on the physical world to attend the burial: 'If only I could nudge you from this sleep, / My maimed darling, my skittery pigeon' - the tenderness and the grotesquerie together - and then a list of plants and birds, 'the bead-drops' and 'the solemn birds', is asked to 'mourn her'. In the final lines the speaker withdraws the claim he has been making: 'Over this damp grave I speak the words my people said, / My father's people, the Pennsylvania Dutch: / 'Dark is the day, dark is the night, / Dark is the grave where my love lies.'' And the last line, set apart, concedes the poem's limits: 'I am not her father, nor she my daughter.' The admission is what makes the poem an elegy rather than a love poem: the grief is real and the relation is not, and the teacher's mourning has to find its justification in the girl's own worth rather than in a family claim.
narrative_structure: Six quatrains and a single separated line; the quatrains are unrhymed but strongly metrical, and the poem moves from memory to invocation to the borrowed funeral formula to the final withdrawal; the last line stands alone as a correction of everything before it.
literary_form: Poem (six quatrains and a closing line)
meter_and_prosody: A formal, almost Latinised diction ('assuage', 'maimed darling', 'skittery pigeon') set beside colloquial and dialectal words ('pickerel smile', 'tendrils', 'bead-drops'); heavy stresses and long vowels give the poem its ceremonial pace, and the plant and bird lists give it the structure of a pastoral elegy in miniature.
historical_context: The Waking (1953) was Roethke's Pulitzer Prize volume; 'Elegy for Jane' belongs to his poems about teaching, written during his years at the University of Washington, and to the tradition of the pastoral elegy that runs from Milton's Lycidas through Whitman's 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'; its Pennsylvania Dutch funeral formula points to the poet's German immigrant background.
literary_significance: One of Roethke's most frequently anthologised poems and his best-known elegy; it is a standard text in courses on the elegy and on the American poem of the 1950s, and its final line is often quoted as an example of the ethical care that distinguishes his work from the confessional poets who followed him.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Waking: Poems 1933-1953 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1953). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the impropriety of grief: a teacher may not mourn a student as a father mourns a daughter, and the poem's honesty lies in its final admission that he has no such right. Around that admission gather the poem's other subjects - the classroom as a place of intense, unspoken attachments, the natural world as the only available language for consolation, and the Pennsylvania Dutch funeral formula that the speaker borrows to give his grief a communal form. The girl herself is made present through details of hair, movement and laughter rather than through character, which is both a limit and a tenderness.
summary: Six unrhymed quatrains and a single final line in which the speaker addresses the dead student, recalls her presence in his classroom - her 'neckcurls, limp and damp as tendrils', her quick laugh - calls on the plants and birds to mourn her, and ends by saying that he has no right to her name.
critical_context: Criticism has concentrated on the poem's management of the teacher's improper grief, on its pastoral machinery and on the final line as an act of self-correction; feminist readings have asked what it means for a male teacher to make a dead girl the object of his elegy, and the poem is often taught alongside Bishop's 'Sestina' and Lowell's 'For the Union Dead' as a study in the limits of elegiac speech.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in the anthologies and study sources consulted; the poem's subtitle and closing line were checked against more than one transcription.

title: I Knew a Woman
description: A poem from Words for the Wind (1958) in which Roethke remembers a woman whose body and movements were 'like a dance', puns his way through the language of measurement and of sexual pleasure, and ends by asking to 'learn how to move'.
plot_or_argument: 'I knew a woman, lovely in her bones, / When small birds sighed, she would sigh back at them; / Ah, when she moved, she moved more ways than one: / The shapes a bright container can contain! / Of her choice virtues only gods should speak, / Or English poets who grew up on Greek / (I'd have them howl in harmony) - / Once I have come to love, I am a fool / For all sweet things.' The opening lines set the poem's method: physical praise ('lovely in her bones') in a diction that keeps turning the woman into an object of measurement - a 'bright container' that can contain shapes - while the speaker admits his own foolishness. The middle stanzas catalogue her movements and her effect on him: 'She played it quick, she played it light and loose; / My eyes, they dazzled, and my heart undone.' The fourth stanza makes the poem's most extraordinary sexual pun - 'immodest modesty', the 'sweetly' of her laughter, and the comparison of her body to a 'bright container' and to a metrical foot - and the last stanza asks for what the poem has been describing: 'She who bears the light / Must bear it in her body; / Take from her, take from me, / And learn how to move.' The poem ends with an imperative that is also a request to be taught, and its final word - 'move' - returns to the dance of the first stanza, so that the poem's argument is that love is a way of moving, learned from the beloved.
narrative_structure: Five five-line stanzas, each rhyming loosely on interlocking sounds rather than a fixed scheme; the poem's sentences run across stanza breaks and the last stanza turns from description to petition, so that the five-line unit becomes the poem's unit of measurement as well as its form.
meter_and_prosody: Punning, propulsive verse in loose pentameters, full of internal rhyme, repetition and circumlocution ('a bright container can contain'); the diction mixes the erotic and the geometrical, the colloquial and the bardic, and the whole poem has the swing of a dance tune.
historical_context: Words for the Wind (1958) gathered The Waking with new poems and won the National Book Award; 'I Knew a Woman' belongs to Roethke's love poems of the mid-1950s and to the period in which he was writing his most openly sensual verse, a period also marked by his teaching at the University of Washington and his travels in Europe.
literary_significance: One of Roethke's best-loved poems and his frankest love poem; it is paired in the Norton Anthology with 'The Waking' and 'Elegy for Jane' and is a frequent anthology piece for its wit and its rhythm, and it is regularly cited as evidence that the 'confessional' generation learned its frankness from him.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Words for the Wind (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1958). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a love poem built on measurement: 'I knew a woman' means both knew her and knew her in the biblical sense, and the poem keeps translating the woman's body into quantity - the 'bright container', the metre, the 'five' of the stanzas - while insisting that her quality escapes it. Its wit about sex is unusually frank for American poetry of 1958, and its final request to be taught how to move makes the woman the poet's master, which reverses the usual hierarchy of the love lyric and gives the poem much of its tenderness.
summary: Five five-line stanzas, in loose iambic pentameter with interlaced rhyme, in which the speaker recalls a woman who 'played' him as an instrument, who 'turned, and turned, and turned' in his arms, and whose 'eyes' and 'sighs' he measures in a language that mixes the erotic with the geometric.
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as Roethke's most successful erotic lyric and as a poem about the impossibility of describing a woman without turning her into a measure or a form; its puns and its repetitions have been analysed as a deliberate imitation of the movement it praises, and it is often compared with Yeats's love poems and with Donne's.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in anthologies and study sources consulted; the poem's stanza form and rhymes were checked against more than one transcription.

title: At the Fishhouses
description: A poem first published in The New Yorker in 1947 and collected in North and South (1946) and then in Poems: North & South - A Cold Spring (1955): a walk past the fishhouses of a Nova Scotia harbour, an old fisherman salting herring, a cormorant on a rock and the cold water of the Atlantic, ending in a meditation on knowledge, total immersion and belief.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens in the present tense and with a painter's eye: 'Although it is a cold evening, / down by one of the fishhouses / an old man sits netting his nets, / his net is almost invisible, a dark purple-brown, / and his shuttle worn and polished.' The light is falling, the herring are heaped in the tubs, and the old man's hands are described with the precision of a still life: 'I have seen him / a hundred times, and he is always there, / and I know he is a 'old man''. The speaker has known this harbour since childhood - 'my grandfather was a fisherman' - and she watches the sea and the light on the water, the seals 'like thick, / dark, / rough stones', and a single cormorant on a rock 'with a kind of / rapt, / awkward dignity'. The poem then passes from description to argument: the sea is 'cold dark deep and absolutely clear, / element bearable to no mortal, / to fish and to seals', and to the speaker's memory of swimming in it as a child, of the 'icy' water and of being 'drenched' in it. In the last two sections the sea becomes the ground of a theory of knowledge: 'It is like what we imagine knowledge to be: / dark, salt, clear, moving, utterly free, / drawn from the cold hard mouth / of the world, derived forever / from the rocky breasts / forever, flowing and drawn, and since / our knowledge is historical, flowing, and flown.' The poem ends on that triple movement - flowing, drawn, flown - which is also the poem's own movement from scene to idea to the human history that holds them.
narrative_structure: Seven sections of irregular length, in long unrhymed lines of variable measure; the poem moves from description to memory to meditation, and its sections are marked by shifts of focus rather than by argument; the final section lifts the whole poem into abstraction while keeping the physical detail ('the cold hard mouth / of the world') in view.
meter_and_prosody: Bishop's characteristic long free-verse line, paced by commas and semicolons rather than by regular stresses; exact colour words ('dark purple-brown', 'silver', 'opaque') and precise verbs ('netting', 'scaling', 'drawn'); flat, unemphatic statement that gives way, in the last lines, to a cadence that is close to prayer.
historical_context: Written in Nova Scotia in the summer of 1946, on Bishop's first return to Great Village since childhood, and published in The New Yorker in 1947; North and South (1946) had appeared in the same year, and the poem belongs to the postwar American poetry of place and to Bishop's lifelong preoccupation with the relation between observation and knowledge.
literary_significance: One of Bishop's most admired poems and the one that established her as a major poet in the eyes of critics such as Randall Jarrell and Robert Lowell; it is a standard anthology text and is central to the critical account of her as a poet of exact description and of the ethics of seeing, and its closing lines on knowledge are among the most discussed in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker in 1947 and collected in Poems: North & South - A Cold Spring (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1955); it appeared in North and South (1946) in some accounts of the volume's contents, and the date given in the Norton list is 1947. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: 'At the Fishhouses' is a poem about the conditions of knowledge, and it reaches that subject through an exact account of a place: the light, the nets, the wood, the salt, the water. Bishop's sea is not a symbol in the ordinary sense but a physical element that is 'bearable to no mortal', and the poem's argument is that knowing is like entering it - cold, total, and impossible to remain in. The old man and the harbour stand for a way of life that history is ending ('our knowledge is historical, flowing, and flown'), and the poem holds together nostalgia, exactness and a religious vocabulary ('element bearable to no mortal') without resolving them.
summary: Seven sections of long-lined free verse in which the speaker describes the light, a row of fishhouses, an old man scaling herring with his knife, the benches and the tubs of salt, the harbour seals and a cormorant, and then rows out to the idea of the sea as 'cold dark deep and absolutely clear', 'element bearable to no mortal', and of knowledge as something one must immerse in.
critical_context: Readings of the poem have concentrated on the relation between description and abstraction - the way the poem earns its last lines by the exactness of its first - and on the politics of the harbour, in which the old fisherman's labour is passing. Feminist and postcolonial critics have written about Bishop's position as an American observer in Nova Scotia, and the poem's final definition of knowledge as 'historical, flowing, and flown' has been central to accounts of her epistemology.
research_notes: There is a discrepancy between the composition date (1946, Nova Scotia) and the date of first periodical publication (1947); the list follows the periodical date. The volume in which the poem first appeared in book form is given as 1955 in the sources consulted, but the Norton list's 1947 implies an earlier appearance, which was not verified.

title: Questions of Travel
description: The title poem of Questions of Travel (1965), first published in The New Yorker on 14 January 1956: two stanzas of tourist cliché about waterfalls, mountains and crowded cities are followed by a long, sceptical meditation on whether travel is 'a dream' or a duty.
plot_or_argument: 'There are too many waterfalls here; the crowded streams / hurry too rapidly down to the sea, / and the pressure of so many clouds on the mountaintops / makes them look like the soft, / smoke-billowing craters / of a 'really magnificent' volcano.' The poem begins in the voice of the disappointed tourist, complete with quotation marks around 'really magnificent', and the first stanzas pile up the sights until they become oppressive: the waterfalls, the rivers, the mountains, the 'big ships, / the little ships, / and the ferry-boats', the 'thousands' of people. Then the poem turns: 'Is it lack of imagination that makes us come / to imagined places, not just stay at home? / Or could the weather be / a delight, a necessity?' In the fourth stanza the speaker admits the dream-logic of travel - 'Oh, must we dream our dreams and have them, too?' - and in the fifth the poem asks the question of its title: 'Should we have stayed at home and thought of here? / Should we be contemplating the long, / long, sun-bright beaches / of Brazil, or the ancient / rock-cut tombs / of Egypt?' The poem does not answer. It ends instead with a domestic image - a child playing with 'the / small, / complicated, / toy' of the world - and with the ambivalence intact: travel is a form of dreaming, and the dream is both an escape and a failure of the imagination that could have conjured the place at home.
narrative_structure: Five irregular stanzas of free verse, with the first two built on accumulation and quoted tourist language, the third and fourth on the turn to question, and the fifth returning to the accumulation of places as a question; the poem's movement is circular rather than progressive, which is its argument.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational and deliberately flat, with exclamations and quotation marks used as irony ('really magnificent', 'the big ships, / the little ships'); precise enumeration and line breaks that isolate single words ('a / child', 'the'); a tone that moves from the jaunty to the meditative without changing register.
historical_context: First published in The New Yorker on 14 January 1956 and collected in Questions of Travel (1965); written during Bishop's years in Brazil (1951-67), where she lived with Lota de Macedo Soares, and belongs to the postwar boom in American travel writing and to the debate about the tourist gaze that would become central to later cultural criticism.
literary_significance: One of Bishop's most quoted poems and the title poem of her third book; it is a standard anthology text and a touchstone for criticism on travel, tourism and the ethics of observation, and it is often taught beside 'In the Waiting Room' as evidence of her interest in the limits of the observing self.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 14 January 1956; collected in Questions of Travel (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the ethics and epistemology of tourism: the traveller wants the real place and brings a stock of images to it, and Bishop renders that contradiction in a poem that is half a travel poster and half an attack on travel posters. 'Should we have stayed at home and thought of here?' is not a rhetorical question but a genuine one, and the poem's answer - that the imagination is both what drives us out and what prevents us from seeing - has made it central to later writing on travel and on the postcolonial tourist. The Brazilian material also belongs to Bishop's own migration, and the poem is a quiet record of an American in the southern hemisphere.
summary: Five stanzas in loose free verse in which the poet describes the postcard beauties of a foreign country - 'there are too many waterfalls here', the 'fat brown rivers', the 'really magnificent' mountains - then turns to the question of why one travels at all, admits 'Oh, must we dream our dreams and have them, too?', and asks 'Should we have stayed at home and thought of here?'
critical_context: Critics have read the poem as a critique of the tourist's desire for authenticity, pointing to the quotation marks around 'really magnificent' as the poem's way of putting the language of tourism in evidence; others have emphasised its Brazilian context and Bishop's own position as an American in Brazil, and the poem has become a standard text in postcolonial and travel-writing criticism.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in anthologies and study sources consulted; the New Yorker date was confirmed by a separate search of the poem's publication history.

title: The Armadillo
description: A poem from Questions of Travel (1965), written in 1956-57 and published in 1957: a night of festival fire balloons over a Brazilian landscape ends with a small armadillo burning, and the poem is dedicated to Robert Lowell, who answered it with 'Skunk Hour'.
plot_or_argument: 'Now and then one of these fire balloons goes up / and, rising, seems to be a star / or a planet. / It is a paper house, a lantern, / with a flame in it.' The poem describes the Brazilian festival practice of sending up small paper balloons with candles inside, which drift over the hills at night like 'a kite' or a 'moon'. The first stanza tracks one balloon up and away, and the second follows another as it begins to come down, over the 'tall, pale, / fireflies' and the mountains, until it disappears. In the third stanza the speaker finds the place where one fell: 'Last night I saw a fire balloon / crash and burn in the hillside, / and the fire went out, / and the armadillo / came out of the ground / and the bushes.' The poem's final image is the animal with its 'rosy, / rabbit-like' ears and its 'weak, / armored' body, and the nest of rabbits 'all / in a ball' beneath it, burnt: 'a weak, / mailed, / baby, / its / poor / little / face / ... ' The poem ends on the failure of the beautiful thing - the fire balloon - which turns out to be a weapon, and on the small creatures that have no idea of the danger above them.
narrative_structure: Three nine-line stanzas of free verse, with the first two describing the balloons and the third turning to the aftermath; the shift is from the vertical movement of the balloons to the horizontal ground where the burnt animal lies, and the last stanza slows into a list of the rabbits' bodies.
meter_and_prosody: Exact, painterly notation and a tone of unemphatic reportage; long lines broken by commas and dashes, with the poet's characteristic use of the dash for an aside or a recoil; the diction is plain until the last lines, where the short words ('weak, / mailed, / baby') and the line breaks do the emotional work.
historical_context: Written in Brazil in 1956-57 and published in 1957, collected in Questions of Travel (1965); it is dedicated to Robert Lowell, and Lowell's 'Skunk Hour' (1958) is dedicated to Bishop in return; the two poems are the central documents of the exchange between the poets about the limits of the 'confessional' mode.
literary_significance: One of Bishop's most anthologised poems and the one most closely tied to her friendship with Lowell; it is the standard text for discussions of the poet's political and ethical responsibilities, and its image of the armadillo has become one of the best-known in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1957 and collected in Questions of Travel (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1965); the Norton list gives 1957 as the date of first publication. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the innocence of beauty and the damage it does: the fire balloons are lovely, and they are also a fire that falls on animals. Bishop does not moralise, and the poem's power comes from the equal weight given to the aesthetic pleasure of the first two stanzas and the cruelty of the last, so that the reader is implicated in enjoying the spectacle. The dedication to Lowell places the poem in a dialogue about the poet's obligation to suffering, and the armadillo - armoured, weak, 'rosy' and defenceless - became the poem's emblem for the vulnerable creature in a beautiful and indifferent world.
summary: Three nine-line stanzas of free verse in which the speaker watches paper fire balloons drift over the mountains, sees one fall into a hillside, and finds in the morning a burnt armadillo and a nest of baby rabbits among the ashes.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as Bishop's answer to Lowell's 'Skunk Hour' and as her most direct statement about the poet's relation to suffering; the fire balloons have been discussed as images of art, of festivity and of the destructive beauty of the Brazilian landscape, and the poem's refusal to console has been central to the critical account of her difference from the confessional poets.
research_notes: The place of first publication in 1957 was not identified with certainty in the sources consulted; the composition date of 1956-57 and the dedication to Lowell are documented, and the date of 1957 follows the Norton list.

title: In the Waiting Room
description: A poem first published in The New Yorker in 1971 and collected in Geography III (1976), in which the six-year-old Elizabeth, waiting in a dentist's waiting room in Worcester, Massachusetts, in February 1918, hears her aunt cry out in pain and is overwhelmed by the knowledge that she is herself - a separate, mortal person, one of 'them'.
plot_or_argument: 'In Worcester, Massachusetts, / I went with Aunt Consuelo / to keep her dentist's appointment / and sat and waited for her / in the dentist's waiting room. / It was winter. It got dark / early.' The opening is deliberately flat and exact: a place, a date (3 February 1918), an aunt, a waiting room, a copy of the National Geographic with 'a dead man slung on a pole' and 'black, naked women' with 'horrifying' breasts. The child reads and waits, and then hears 'an oh! of pain' from the inner office: 'It was me. / ... my aunt was crying out'. The shock is that the aunt's voice is her own voice, and the poem's central stanzas record the child's vertigo: 'I said to myself: three days / and you'll be seven years old. / I was saying it to stop / the sensation of falling off / the round, turning world / into cold, blue-black space.' She looks at the waiting room as if from outside, at the 'other people' - 'What similarities - / boots, hands, the family voice / I felt in my throat, or even / the National Geographic / and those awful hanging breasts - / held us all together / or made us all just one?' The poem's climax is the recognition 'you are an I, / you are an Elizabeth, / you are one of them', and its ending is a return: 'Then I was back in it. / The War was on. Outside, / in Worcester, Massachusetts, / were night and slush and cold, / and it was still the fifth / of February, 1918.'
narrative_structure: Nine stanzas of unequal length, from four lines to more than twenty, in loose free verse; the poem moves from external description to interior monologue and back, and its stanzas are marked by shifts in the child's attention; the last stanza returns to the outside world and closes the frame opened by the first.
meter_and_prosody: Bishop's late free verse at its most exact and least rhetorical: short declarative sentences, reported speech and quotation marks, a child's diction and a child's non sequiturs, and a rhythm that follows breath and attention rather than metre; the poem's horror is produced by plain statement ('It was me') and its comfort by the flat particularity of the last lines.
historical_context: First published in The New Yorker in July 1971 - Bishop's first new poem in some years - and collected in Geography III (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976), which won the National Book Critics Circle Award; the poem's date, 5 February 1918, places it in Bishop's seventh year, and its Worcester setting is the city of her birth, which she had left as a small child.
literary_significance: The poem that reopened Bishop's career after a long silence and one of the most admired American poems of the 1970s; it is central to the critical account of her late style and is regularly taught as a study of childhood consciousness and of the autobiographical poem, and it is her selection in the Norton Anthology alongside 'One Art'.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker in July 1971; collected in Geography III (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the birth of self-consciousness, and it locates that birth in a moment of identification with another person's pain: the child discovers that she is separate because she hears her aunt's cry as her own. Bishop's interest is in the paradox that the sense of being an 'I' arrives as a fall - 'falling off / the round, turning world / into cold, blue-black space' - and that identity is both a horror and a bond: the 'family voice' in the throat is what makes the child one of 'them'. The National Geographic material adds the postcolonial and the sexual: the naked women and the 'dead man slung on a pole' are the child's first images of a wider world, and her recoil from them is part of the same recognition of a body that is vulnerable and exposed.
summary: Nine stanzas of free verse, mostly unrhymed, in which the child reads a National Geographic while her aunt is in the dentist's chair, looks at the photographs of volcanoes and of naked women, hears a cry of pain, and falls into a trance of self-recognition before returning to the ordinary street outside.
critical_context: Criticism has concentrated on the poem's treatment of identity as both a fall and a bond, on the National Geographic images as the child's introduction to race, gender and history, and on Bishop's difference from the confessional poets: the poem exposes a childhood trauma, but it does so with the same reticence and exactness as her descriptions of landscape, and the 'I' is constructed as a character rather than confessed.
research_notes: The exact day of the New Yorker appearance in July 1971 was not verified; the month and year come from a search of the poem's publication history, and the text was read through the anthologies and study sources consulted.

title: One Art
description: A villanelle first published in The New Yorker on 26 April 1976 and collected in Geography III (1976): the poet instructs herself in the art of losing, from keys and hours to a continent and a loved one, and the form's refrains register the discipline cracking.
plot_or_argument: 'The art of losing isn't hard to master; / so many things seem filled with the intent / to be lost that their loss is no disaster.' The poem begins with a maxim that sounds like consolation and is actually a command: lose things, and do it well. The examples grow steadily larger - door keys, an hour badly spent, names, a mother's watch, two beloved cities, a continent, 'and, vaster, / some realms I owned, two rivers, a continent' - and with each the instruction becomes more insistent: 'Lose something every day. Accept the fluster / of lost door keys, the hour badly spent. / The art of losing isn't hard to master.' The fake-serious tone is the poem's engine: the villanelle's refrains repeat like a lesson being learned by rote, and the poet's 'practice' of loss is also a practice of the form. Then, in the fifth stanza, the poem reaches the loss it cannot absorb: 'I lost two cities, lovely ones. And, vaster, / some realms I owned, two rivers, a continent. / I miss them, but it wasn't a disaster.' The last stanza turns to the beloved - 'Even losing you (the joking voice, a gesture / I love) I shan't have lied. It's evident / the art of losing's not too hard to master / though it may look like (Write it!) like disaster.' The parenthesis is the poem's breakdown: the poet has to command herself to write the word 'disaster', and the repetition of 'like' shows the simile and the composure failing at the same moment.
narrative_structure: A villanelle: five tercets and a closing quatrain, nineteen lines in all, with two refrains that recur alternately; the refrains are varied - 'isn't hard to master' becomes 'not too hard to master' - and the rhymes (master/disaster, intent/spent, gesture/master) are carried by assonance and by the poem's repeated vocabulary rather than by exact rhyme.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, dry, almost prosaic in diction, with exclamations and parentheses that dramatise the speaker's struggle for composure ('(Write it!)'); the line is loose iambic pentameter, and the poem's flatness is the point: the tone is that of someone giving herself instructions, and the poetry is in the mask slipping.
historical_context: First published in The New Yorker on 26 April 1976 and collected in Geography III (1976); Bishop wrote as many as eight drafts of the poem over years, and it belongs to the last period of her life, when she was teaching at Harvard, ill with asthma and separated from Alice Methfessel. It is one of the poems that revived the villanelle in late twentieth-century English verse.
literary_significance: Bishop's best-known poem and one of the most admired villanelles in English; it is the poem through which her work is most often introduced, it is central to every account of her late style and of the modern revival of the villanelle, and it is universally anthologised, in the Norton Anthology and outside it.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 26 April 1976; collected in Geography III (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1976). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the discipline of loss and the impossibility of that discipline: its instructional voice is a defence against grief, and the villanelle's repetitions, which sound like mastery, are what betray it. 'The art of losing' is the art of making loss into form, and the poem both performs and mistrusts that transformation; the 'joking voice' it addresses belongs to Alice Methfessel, from whom Bishop was separated when she wrote the poem, and the small domestic losses of the opening become the measure of the large one at the end, so that the poem's scale is one of its subjects.
summary: Nineteen lines in five tercets and a quatrain, with two refrains - 'The art of losing isn't hard to master' and 'It's evident / the art of losing's not too hard to master / though it may look like (Write it!) like disaster' - in which a series of losses, each larger than the last, is met with consoling imperatives.
critical_context: The poem's criticism has concentrated on the relation between form and feeling - the villanelle's repetitions as an image of the mind circling grief - and on the autobiographical occasion in Bishop's separation from Alice Methfessel; the surviving drafts, discussed by Bishop's editors and biographers, show her working towards the parenthesis '(Write it!)', which is now treated as one of the great moments of twentieth-century American poetry.
research_notes: The number of drafts (given here as 'as many as eight') is reported in the sources consulted and was not checked against the manuscripts; the dating of the New Yorker appearance is from a search of the poem's publication history and agrees with the Norton list.

title: A Streetcar Named Desire
description: The play that opened on Broadway on 3 December 1947: Blanche DuBois, a schoolteacher from Laurel, Mississippi, comes to her sister Stella's two-room flat in the French Quarter of New Orleans, and the brutal, tender world of her brother-in-law Stanley Kowalski destroys her illusions and finally her mind.
plot_or_argument: Blanche DuBois arrives at the Elysian Fields, the shabby quarter of New Orleans where her sister Stella lives in two rooms with her husband Stanley Kowalski, carrying a suitcase of clothes and a trunk of papers; she has lost the family plantation, Belle Reve, and has been dismissed from her teaching job in Laurel, Mississippi. She is horrified by the flat, the neighbourhood and Stanley, and she sets about trying to improve Stella's life and to arrest her own decline: she drinks, she bathes constantly, she avoids strong light and she flirts with Stanley's friend Mitch, a gentle, unmarried man who lives with his dying mother. Stanley, who has been checking on Blanche's story, discovers that she was dismissed for an affair with a student, that she has been living in a hotel in Laurel and that she has been promiscuous since; he tells Mitch, who abandons her. Stella goes into labour; while Stanley and Stella are at the hospital, Blanche, left alone in the flat, is raped by Stanley. In the last scene the family and the doctor and matron wait while Blanche, who has lost her grip on reality, is taken to a mental institution; she goes with the doctor with the line 'Whoever you are - I have always depended on the kindness of strangers.' The play's famous other elements - the poker game, the streetcar named Desire that brings Blanche to the quarter and the one named Cemeteries, the Varsouviana polka that plays in her head, the paper lantern she puts over the light bulb, Stanley's cry of 'Stella!' - carry its themes as much as its dialogue does.
narrative_structure: Eleven scenes rather than acts, moving without interval through a single set that represents both the Kowalskis' two rooms and the street outside; the play's time is compressed into a few months and its action is organised around a series of confrontations - the poker night, the birthday party, the revelation of the past, the rape - with expressionist devices (music, light, the paper lantern, the offstage streetcar) carrying the inner life.
principal_characters: Blanche DuBois, a former schoolteacher from Laurel, Mississippi, who has lost Belle Reve and her reputation and lives by illusion; Stella Kowalski, her younger sister, who has chosen Stanley and the Quarter over her sister; Stanley Kowalski, a Polish American factory worker and bowler, sensual, brutal and shrewd; Harold 'Mitch' Mitchell, Stanley's friend, who courts Blanche and abandons her when he learns of her past; Eunice Hubbell, the upstairs neighbour; Allan Grey, Blanche's dead husband, present only in memory; Steve Hubbell and Pablo Gonzales, the poker players; a young collector, a nurse and a doctor in the last scene.
meter_and_prosody: A lyrical, image-rich dialogue that lifts Southern speech into poetry; long monologues and confession scenes for Blanche, short brutal exchanges for Stanley; extensive stage directions that function as prose poems; the sound of the Varsouviana polka and the streetcar used as musical motifs, and light used symbolically throughout.
historical_context: Premiered on Broadway at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre on 3 December 1947, directed by Elia Kazan, with Jessica Tandy as Blanche, Kim Hunter as Stella, Marlon Brando as Stanley and Karl Malden as Mitch; it won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1948 and was published by New Directions in 1947. Its Southern Gothic setting, its frankness about sex and its Method-acting production made it the defining American play of the immediate postwar years, and the 1951 film, also directed by Kazan, fixed it in popular culture.
literary_significance: One of the two or three most important American plays of the twentieth century and the work through which Williams's reputation is measured; it is a standard text in the study of American drama, of Southern literature and of tragedy in a modern setting, and its characters - Blanche, Stanley, Stella - have become cultural archetypes.
bibliographical_notes: First published by New Directions (New York, 1947); premiered at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre, New York, on 3 December 1947. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The play's central subject is the collision between illusion and desire: Blanche lives by illusions - of gentility, of purity, of art and of the past - and Stanley lives by an appetite that is honest, brutal and destructive. Williams makes both attractive and both damaging, and refuses the moral comfort of choosing between them; the Southern past, with Belle Reve and its 'epic fornications', is present as a burden and a lie, and the play's treatment of sexuality - Blanche's promiscuity, her husband's homosexuality and suicide, Stanley's rape - was among the frankest on the American stage of its time. Its other subject is the vulnerability of women in a world of male violence and male codes, and the final image of Blanche led away is an indictment as much of the society that has no place for her as of Stanley.
summary: Eleven scenes, a single set of two rooms and a bath in the Elysian Fields, five characters - Blanche, Stella, Stanley, Mitch and the neighbour Eunice - and a plot that moves from Blanche's arrival, through the poker night, the courtship by Mitch, the revelation of her past in Laurel, the rape, and the final removal to the state asylum.
critical_context: Criticism has read the play through the Southern Gothic tradition, through psychoanalysis (Blanche's narcissism, Stanley's brutality, the play's Oedipal undercurrents), through gender and queer theory (the homosexuality of Blanche's dead husband Allan Grey and the play's treatment of masculinity) and through class (the decline of the plantation aristocracy and the rise of the immigrant working class). Its staging history, from Kazan's production to later revivals, is a central topic of American theatre scholarship, and the 1951 film's censorship of the rape has been much discussed.

title: The Swimmer
description: A story first published in The New Yorker on 18 July 1964 and collected in The Brigadier and the Golf Widow the same year: on a bright Sunday in midsummer, Neddy Merrill decides to swim home across Westchester County through his neighbours' pools, and the afternoon turns into a journey through a whole life and its losses.
plot_or_argument: The story opens in high summer: 'It was one of those midsummer Sundays when everyone sits around saying, I drank too much last night.' Neddy Merrill, hungover and happy, is at a party with his wife Lucinda, and the idea comes to him - 'Making his way home by an uncommon route' - that he will swim home through the pools of the neighbourhood, the Bunkers', the Levys', the Welchers' (whose pool is empty), the Hallorans', the Sachses', the Biswangers', Shirley Adams's, and so home. The first pools are festive, full of friends and drinks, and Neddy is a man in excellent shape who 'might have been described as a hearty man'; but the signs accumulate. The Welchers' pool is dry and their house is for sale. The Hallorans, an elderly couple, receive him naked and mention, in passing, that his children have been in trouble. At the Biswangers' party he is treated as an intruder. Shirley Adams, once his mistress, is cool to him. The light changes, the leaves blow, and by the time Neddy reaches his own house it is dark, the doors are locked and the house is empty: 'He shouted, pounded on the door, tried to force it with his shoulder, and then, looking in at the windows, saw that the place was empty.'
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative with no chapter or scene breaks, moving from pool to pool in a strictly linear way; the passage of time is registered almost entirely through the weather, the light, the leaves and the behaviour of the people, and the reader is left to infer the discrepancy between Neddy's experience and the truth.
meter_and_prosody: A lucid, elegant, faintly ironic third-person prose that keeps a straight face while the events turn impossible; exact social notation (drinks, wet hair, tennis shoes, the names of the pools); a habit of mythic or apocalyptic imagery inside an ordinary scene; and a closing sentence that refuses explanation.
historical_context: Published in The New Yorker on 18 July 1964 and collected in The Brigadier and the Golf Widow (1964) and The Stories of John Cheever (1978); Cheever had conceived the story originally as a novel and had written some 150 pages of notes before reducing it to a story, and its Westchester setting and its suburban swimming pools belong to the landscape of his own life at Ossining, New York.
literary_significance: Cheever's most anthologised story and a standard text in the American short-story canon; its fantastic premise and its treatment of time have made it a favourite of critics and of teachers of fiction, and the 1968 film with Burt Lancaster, from a screenplay by Eleanor Perry, gave it a second life.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The New Yorker, 18 July 1964; collected in The Brigadier and the Golf Widow (New York: Harper and Row, 1964) and in The Stories of John Cheever (New York: Knopf, 1978). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is an American fable of the man who refuses to see that his life has collapsed: Neddy's swim is a journey through time disguised as a journey through space, and the pools measure out his losses - money, friends, a mistress, his children, his house, his wife - while he experiences them as a single afternoon of pleasure. Cheever's subject is the suburban middle class and its self-deception, and the story's fantastic premise is the vehicle for a realistic account of failure; the name 'Lucinda River' turns the swim into a mock-epic journey, and the empty house at the end is a judgment delivered without a moralist.
summary: A single continuous narrative in which Neddy Merrill, 'a slender man' in his forties, sets out from a pool party at the Westerhazys' to swim the eight miles home through a chain of private pools he names the 'Lucinda River' after his wife, and finds at each pool a colder season, a drier welcome and more of his life gone.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a modern myth of the fall, as a portrait of suburban self-deception, and as a formal experiment in which the narrative's temporality is the plot's real subject; Cheever's own notes and the 1968 film are frequently discussed, and the story is often compared with Fitzgerald's Gatsby and with Joyce's 'The Dead' as a study of a man who fails to understand his own life.
