title: Those Winter Sundays
description: A poem from A Ballad of Remembrance (1962) in which an adult remembers his father getting up in the blueblack cold of Sunday mornings to bank the fires and polish his good shoes before church, and regrets that as a child he never thanked him for the labour that made the house warm.
plot_or_argument: 'Sundays too my father got up early / and put his clothes on in the blueblack cold, / then with cracked hands that ached / from labor in the weekday weather made / banked fires blaze. No one ever thanked him.' The first sentence establishes the poem's whole situation: the father's habitual, unthanked labour, performed before dawn on the one day of rest. The second stanza moves inside the house - 'I'd wake and hear the cold splintering, breaking' - and the child waits, hearing the house warm and the father call, until 'slowly I would rise and dress, / fearing the chronic angers of that house'. The third stanza turns to the poem's other detail: 'Speaking indifferently to him, / who had driven out the cold / and polished my good shoes as well.' The single rhyme of the poem, 'cold'/'shoes as well' in the third stanza (and 'ach-ed'/'thanked' in the first), does its work quietly, and the last line, set apart, is the poem's whole meaning: 'What did I know, what did I know / of love's austere and lonely offices?' The repetition of the question is not a rhetorical flourish but a confession that the knowledge came too late, and 'offices' - both duties and church services - joins the father's Sunday labour to the language of the church he was preparing his family for.
narrative_structure: Three quatrains and a single separated line; the quatrains are unrhymed except for the assonantal 'ached'/'thanked' and the rhyme of 'cold' with the third stanza's end, and the poem's movement is from the father's actions to the boy's fear to the adult's regret, with the final line turning the description into a question.
literary_form: Poem (three quatrains and a closing line)
meter_and_prosody: Plain, exact, unadorned free verse with heavy stresses and a sparse syntax; the diction is domestic and physical ('blueblack cold', 'cracked hands', 'banked fires', 'the cold splintering'), and the poem's effects are made by line breaks, by the one rhyme and by the repetition of the final question.
historical_context: A Ballad of Remembrance (1962) was Hayden's third collection and the book in which his mature style appeared; the poem belongs to his poems about his Detroit childhood and foster family, and its appearance in the same year as the revised 'Middle Passage' marks the point at which Hayden's historical and domestic poems were being read together. It is one of his most anthologised poems and a staple of American school anthologies.
literary_significance: One of the most widely taught American poems of the twentieth century and Hayden's best-known work; it is a standard text in courses on the American family poem, on African American poetry and on the sonnet-sized lyric, and its final line is among the most quoted in modern American verse.
bibliographical_notes: Published in A Ballad of Remembrance (London: Paul Breman, 1962). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about a love expressed as labour rather than as speech, and about the child's failure to recognise it: the father's 'cracked hands', the 'banked fires' and the polished shoes are the poem's evidence, and the adult speaker's regret is its verdict. Its racial and historical context is present but unnamed - the 'weekday weather' of a Black working man's labour, the 'chronic angers' of a household under pressure - and Hayden's refusal to make the poem a document of protest is precisely what made him a controversial figure in the 1960s; the poem's power comes from its specificity, which is also a kind of representativeness.
summary: Three quatrains and a single closing line, in free verse with one rhyme, in which the father's Sunday labours - lighting fires, polishing shoes, calling the family - are set against the boy's indifference and the poem's final question about 'love's austere and lonely offices'.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as a study in the expression of love through work, as a portrait of Black working-class fatherhood, and as a poem about the belatedness of understanding; the phrase 'love's austere and lonely offices' is regularly discussed as the poem's centre, and the poem's reticence has been central to the argument that Hayden's lyricism was a political as well as an aesthetic choice.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in anthologies and study sources consulted; the poem's stanza form and its single rhyme were checked against more than one transcription.

title: Summertime and the Living . . .
description: A poem from A Ballad of Remembrance (1962) whose title takes its cue from Gershwin's 'Summertime': a series of remembered and imagined scenes of Black childhood and community life in Detroit and the rural South, held together by heat, song and the presence of violence.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens in the heat of a remembered summer and moves through a series of scenes rather than a single narrative: children playing in the street, a woman singing, the 'good times' of a neighbourhood, and, cutting across them, the violence that the community lives with. Its title borrows the opening of Gershwin's aria from Porgy and Bess, and the ellipsis in the title is the poem's point: the song's promise of easy living is broken off before it can be completed. Hayden's scenes are rendered with the same exactness as 'Those Winter Sundays' - the physical detail of heat, water, voices and music - and the poem's structure is musical, returning to its refrain-like images of summer as it moves between the remembered and the reported. The poem's ending does not resolve the tension between the idyll and the violence but holds the two together, which is the characteristic gesture of Hayden's poems of Black American life.
narrative_structure: Four numbered sections of free verse of unequal length, organised by image and by recurrence rather than by narrative; the sections shift between first person and third person and between past and present, and the poem's title functions as a refrain that the sections answer.
meter_and_prosody: A lyric free verse with a strong sense of song, using repetition, refrain-like phrases and the cadences of Black speech and of hymns; the diction is concrete and sensory (heat, dust, water, voices), and the poem's shifts of register - from the conversational to the elegiac - are managed by line breaks and by changes of scene.
historical_context: A Ballad of Remembrance (1962) was published in London by Paul Breman as part of the Heritage series and won the Grand Prix de la Poésie at the first World Festival of Negro Arts in Dakar in 1966; the poem belongs to Hayden's poems of Black American life written before the Black Arts Movement made his reticence controversial, and its Detroit and Southern material reflects his own upbringing in Paradise Valley and his research into his family's Southern past.
literary_significance: One of Hayden's most anthologised poems and the companion to 'Those Winter Sundays' in the Norton selection; it is a standard text for the study of his treatment of childhood and community and for the debate about protest and art in African American poetry of the 1960s.
bibliographical_notes: Published in A Ballad of Remembrance (London: Paul Breman, 1962). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the double life of a Black childhood: the warmth and richness of community and the constant proximity of racial violence. Its Gershwin title points to the way American culture has packaged Black life as song and sunshine, and the poem's four sections restore the history that the song leaves out, without surrendering the pleasure that the song names. Hayden's refusal to choose between celebration and protest is the poem's argument, and it is the reason the poem has been central to discussions of his place between the Black Arts Movement and the earlier protest tradition.
summary: Four sections of free verse in which the speaker remembers a childhood summer - the streets, the porches, the music, the revivals, a woman singing, and the news of a killing - and sets the pleasures of the season against the knowledge of what awaits the children who live in it.
critical_context: Criticism has discussed the poem's use of the Gershwin song as an ironic frame, its structure of lyric scenes and its place in Hayden's argument with the protest poetry of the 1960s; the poem is often read beside 'Those Winter Sundays' as evidence of his range, and its treatment of violence within a lyric idyll has been central to the critical reassessment of his work since the 1980s.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the text and commentary in the sources consulted, and the reading of the Gershwin title is the standard critical one rather than a quotation from Hayden.
